title: Wolf-Rayet 124 (NIRCam and MIRI composite image)
caption: The Wolf-Rayet star WR 124 and its nebula, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: WR 124 · constellation Sagitta · about 15000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Webb ERO Production Team

recognition.text: Official ESA/Webb press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A bright star blazes at the center, marked with the diffraction spikes typical of Webb's Near-infrared Camera. They are caused by the physical structure of the telescope. Around the star spreads a nebula of gas and dust, and background stars and galaxies show through it. The star is Wolf-Rayet 124, or WR 124, a luminous, hot, ageing massive star about 15000 light-years away in Sagitta.

The nebula is made of material the star has thrown off, and its structure records the history of those episodes of mass loss. Instead of smooth shells, it formed from random, lopsided ejections. Bright clumps of gas and dust look like tadpoles swimming toward the star, their tails blown back by its stellar wind.
The two instruments play different roles. NIRCam balances the glare of the star against the fainter material around it, while the Mid-Infrared Instrument, MIRI, brings out the nebula's structure.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.21 x 1.85 arcminutes) and distance (15000 light years), the frame spans roughly 9.6 × 8.1 light-years. Its light set out about 15,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This Webb composite combines near-infrared NIRCam and mid-infrared MIRI data. Within each instrument, shorter wavelengths are shown bluer. The 900 nm, 1.5 μm and 7.7 μm filters appear in blue, 2.1, 3.35 and 11 μm in green, and 4.44, 4.7, 12 and 18 μm in red.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, so these colors are assigned to wavelengths no one could see directly.
